channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Is AI the new cigarettes? Our VC panel digs into Anthropic’s S-1 | E2356
gist: Jason Calacanis's This Week in VC panel (D.A. Wallach of Time BioVentures, Dave McClure of Practical VC, Ben Black of Acadian Ventures/Power Law) dissects Anthropic's S-1: $16.3B first-half revenue, an $80.7B net loss of which $72.4B is non-cash fair-value marks on convertible notes, a 900% net revenue retention figure, and the claim that customers spend ~0.1% of opex on AI. Wallach frames the core question as whether 'intelligence is the new cigarette' (Altria-like addictive, high-margin demand), while the panel also covers compute depreciation, neocloud risk, Calacanis's monthly Bitcoin-is-dead posts, and SPVs crowding out emerging VC funds. The transcript appears to be machine-translated, so some figures are garbled.

insights.claim: Anthropic filed its public S-1 to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, reporting first-half revenue of $16.3 billion, a 14-fold increase from $1.2 billion in the first half of 2025.
insights.speaker: Lon (producer) / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Anthropic's IPO arrives with hypergrowth already in the numbers.
insights.quote: Revenues for the first half of the year amounted to 16.3 billion. This represents a 14-fold increase compared to the 1.2 billion of the first half of 2025.

insights.claim: Anthropic's first-half net loss was $80.7 billion, but $72.4 billion of it came from a non-cash change in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, largely tied to Amazon and Google note purchase agreements, which were marked up as the valuation rose.
insights.speaker: Lon (producer)
insights.so_what: Headline losses are mostly accounting; analysts must strip out fair-value remeasurement to gauge cash burn.
insights.quote: $72.4 billion of that amount was driven by a non-cash accounting charge on convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFE

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal reports Anthropic aims to go public the week of November 16, raising $100 billion or more at a valuation of about $1.5-2 trillion.
insights.speaker: Lon (producer)
insights.so_what: Sets a near-term catalyst and valuation anchor for the AI complex.

insights.claim: Dave McClure says Anthropic appears to have been operationally profitable for the last two quarters but has more than $500 billion of capex-type commitments, including over $100 billion each with Google and Amazon.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Profitability today must be weighed against massive locked-in compute obligations.
insights.quote: It seems like capital spending is insane. That 's more than $500 billion in capital spending.

insights.claim: McClure would value Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion rather than $2-2.5 trillion, and expects its run-rate revenue to reach roughly $150-200 billion next year rather than the previously discussed $300 billion, noting growth has slowed and Replit switched its default model to OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A secondary-market investor sees the top of the IPO range as full; competitive defaults are shifting.

insights.claim: Calacanis warns that Anthropic's widely cited 'ARR' is really an annualized run rate (last month or quarter times 12 or 4), not annual recurring revenue like a subscription business.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Usage-based token revenue is more volatile than SaaS ARR and should be discounted accordingly.
insights.quote: Annualized recurring revenue is for subscription products like Netflix or your Verizon accounts. It is clearly different from this.

insights.claim: Ben Black says the S-1 shows analysts need new metrics because SaaS tools like ARR don't fit a business that sells compute with a margin through multiple models whose costs are all falling.
insights.speaker: Ben Black
insights.so_what: Valuation debates will hinge on which framing public analysts adopt in the first weeks.
insights.quote: we need to have a new set of measures for these businesses

insights.claim: The panel highlights Anthropic's disclosed 900% net revenue retention, meaning the same customer cohort spent nine times more in the same three-month period a year later.
insights.speaker: Ben Black / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Extreme expansion within existing customers is the strongest evidence of demand, but its durability is unknown.
insights.quote: the only number I simply haven't been able to overcome: the 900% net income retention.

insights.claim: Calacanis calls Anthropic possibly the biggest business ever created, noting ~$100 billion of annualized revenue would equal about a quarter of Alphabet's or Apple's revenue and a third of Microsoft's after three or four years of charging.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Bulls frame the IPO valuation against mega-cap revenue scale achieved in record time.
insights.quote: I think this is the biggest business ever created by humans on planet Earth.

themes.theme: Is intelligence the new cigarette? Enterprise AI demand

insights.claim: D.A. Wallach frames the key question for Anthropic as whether intelligence is 'the new cigarette', likening it to Altria/Philip Morris, historically the best stock of the past 100 years thanks to huge gross margins and addictive, unlimited demand.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: If AI usage is habit-forming like tobacco, compounding margins justify extreme valuations.
insights.quote: I think the fundamental question for Anthropic and all the players in this market is basically whether intelligence is the new cigarette, right?

insights.claim: Wallach says the most interesting S-1 number is that customers spend roughly 0.1% of total operating expenses on AI, which bulls read as headroom but which he says raises the question of why spending isn't already higher, suggesting a utility rather than cost constraint.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Low penetration cuts both ways: huge TAM or evidence that usefulness, not price, limits adoption, complicating Jevons-paradox bull cases.
insights.quote: users of our intelligence spend approximately one- tenth of one percent of their total operating expenses on AI today.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues enterprise AI adoption is constrained by 'meat sacks' (employees who can't implement it), citing Uber burning through its token budget in the first quarter and then putting about 30,000 employees on OpenAI at once.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Human implementation capacity, not supply, is the binding constraint on enterprise token spend.
insights.quote: The sacks of meat are blocking this.

insights.claim: Calacanis points to Microsoft offering buyouts to 60,000 people, about one in four employees, as a roadmap for how organizations will restructure around AI.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Large-scale white-collar headcount cuts may accompany AI adoption at incumbents.

insights.claim: Ben Black questions how long customers will pay for frontier models as prices drop once models age and users route work via OpenRouter to cheaper open-source models.
insights.speaker: Ben Black
insights.so_what: Commoditization of trailing models threatens long-run margins for frontier labs.

insights.claim: Wallach dislikes owning Anthropic now because everyone in the world has a huge financial incentive to compete with its product more cheaply.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Being the leader puts a target on Anthropic's pricing power.
insights.quote: everyone in the world has a huge financial incentive to figure out how to compete with your product cheaper.

insights.claim: Wallach says shorting the Anthropic IPO in the short term would make an investor look like an idiot, even though long-term defensibility and profitability questions remain open.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Near-term momentum likely favors the IPO; skepticism is a long-horizon trade.
insights.quote: Be the guy who bets against Anthropic's IPO? You're going to look like an idiot.

insights.claim: OpenAI reportedly has about 50 million paying consumer subscribers out of roughly 900 million weekly users (about 6%), compared with an estimated 110 million paid Microsoft 365 subscribers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Consumer AI conversion is already approaching the scale of the most successful subscription product.

insights.claim: A Harmonic chart shown cites run rates of about $65 billion for Anthropic, $50 billion for OpenAI, $49 billion for Netflix, $40 billion for Salesforce and $27 billion for Adobe.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI labs already out-earn top subscription software franchises, putting Adobe-type incumbents at risk.

insights.claim: Wallach argues Apple deliberately waited on AI, is not wasting money on infrastructure, owns iPhone distribution, and could eventually preload good-enough on-device AI or simply buy a company like Instinct.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Apple's capex restraint could prove a strategic advantage if edge AI becomes good enough.
insights.quote: I think they intentionally decided to wait. I think they are patient. I think they have the distribution, so they're in pole position here.

insights.claim: Wallach expects 99% of what average consumers want from AI to run on-device on iPhones within a few years, while complex multi-agent enterprise workflows stay in the cloud, and says he still refuses to give any AI access to his email.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Privacy and edge compute favor device owners over cloud labs in consumer AI.

insights.claim: McClure says OpenAI is the No. 1 consumer AI platform by usage, Google Gemini No. 2, and Canva No. 3.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Incumbent design apps retain consumer AI reach despite disruption fears.

insights.claim: McClure says Canva's price fell about 25% on the secondary market after a report that its growth slowed from 35% to 20%, amid perceptions that Claude Design is eating into Canva and Figma.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: In AI-era markets, perceived loss of momentum is repriced brutally in private secondaries.
insights.quote: In this world, the perception of losing momentum is everything.

insights.claim: Wallach counters that Figma has network effects since designer teams have collaborated on it for a decade, so Claude Design hasn't eaten its lunch as feared six months ago.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Collaborative workflow lock-in can blunt AI disruption of SaaS tools.
insights.quote: Well, it turns out they have network effects.

themes.theme: Compute economics, neoclouds and founders' motives

insights.claim: McClure says the key unknown is the depreciation life of AI capex: chips may earn for four to six years, but neocloud amortization may be far shorter, while SpaceX's Q3 results showed a sub-12-month payback that Elon Musk thinks can reach six months.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Depreciation assumptions determine whether AI infrastructure earns its cost of capital.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues servers in data centers typically last 7-10 years, with old frontier hardware repurposed to inference, storage and background tasks, so the only cost of keeping them running is human labor.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Longer useful lives would make GPU depreciation fears overstated.
insights.quote: The average lifespan of computing in other data centers is 7, 8, 9 or 10 years for some of these servers.

insights.claim: Wallach says hyperscalers are behaving rationally because they can earn 6-7% on cash and AI capex may return 10-14%, and if it blows up they simply stop spending.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers carry optionality; the real risk sits with leveraged neoclouds.

insights.claim: Wallach argues the circular economy of labs, clouds and hardware providers is coherent, and the only question for the next decade is whether end customers provide enough revenue, so investors should focus on AI's customers rather than the labs.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Track downstream customer revenue, not lab disclosures, to judge AI sustainability.
insights.quote: the only question that matters in the next decade is whether that organism can find enough nutrients in its environment.

insights.claim: McClure avoided neoclouds (and missed CoreWeave) because their cost of capital and deployment timelines are outside their control, and they depend on Nvidia's goodwill, while he views hyperscalers as dominant enough to always adapt.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Neocloud equity carries uncontrollable financing and supplier risk.
insights.quote: All neo labs, your cost of capital is out of your control.

insights.claim: Wallach describes Anthropic's leaders as genuine 'religious extremists' about AI rather than profit-seekers, warning that if they are wrong they could be beaten by businesspeople like Zuckerberg, Nadella and Altman; Oracle's ~$400 billion capex bet may be Larry Ellison's riskiest hand.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Mission-driven leadership may be an asset in research but a liability in a commodity business fight.

insights.claim: Ben Black says Dario Amodei publicly rebuked Sam Altman for reckless compute buying, yet once it became clear locked-in compute was needed to win, Anthropic followed Altman's playbook.
insights.speaker: Ben Black
insights.so_what: Compute hoarding has become table stakes, which explains Anthropic's large commitments.

insights.claim: Calacanis posts monthly that Bitcoin is dead, arguing ETF outflows will continue, its 'Ponzi' evangelism has faded, capital should move to superintelligence, and it will never surpass its all-time high again; he still holds millions in Bitcoin and about $750,000 in Tao.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Even a holder publicly bets against new highs, partly as engagement trolling.
insights.quote: Bitcoin will never surpass its all-time highs again .

insights.claim: Wallach says the crypto bull case has shifted from speculation to a debasement trade in a possibly two-decade inflationary rate environment, but notes gold has fallen over the last six months, making the backdrop unfavorable for debasement assets.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Bitcoin's thesis now rides on secular debasement, which recent gold weakness undercuts.

insights.claim: McClure sees solid use cases in stablecoins, tokenization of real-world assets (e.g. Robinhood) and DeFi lending, but views most other crypto as lacking underlying assets, unlike neocloud loans backed by data centers and GPUs.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Crypto value is migrating to stablecoin and RWA infrastructure rather than speculative tokens.

insights.claim: Calacanis says 10-20 top venture firms are absorbing about 75% of all capital, leaving emerging managers struggling to raise funds and shifting to SPVs, which risks commoditizing fee economics.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Fee compression and SPV proliferation pressure small VC funds.
insights.quote: SPVs are killing the venture capital radio star.

insights.claim: Wallach predicts AI makes entrepreneurship so cheap and leveraged that the best future founders will raise less money, so returns will swing back to small funds writing small checks.
insights.speaker: D.A. Wallach
insights.so_what: Small seed funds may outperform mega-funds in the AI era.
insights.quote: The best entrepreneurs of the coming years are going to raise less money than the best startup founders have raised , okay? Because they don't need it.

insights.claim: Calacanis says capital-efficient 'alicorns' reach revenue fast enough to skip rounds, and he has had to ask several portfolio companies to raise $10-20 million so his fund can secure reserves at $250 million to $1 billion valuations.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Early-stage investors face difficulty deploying follow-on capital into revenue-rich, lean startups.
insights.quote: The future belongs to alicorns

insights.claim: Ben Black's closed-end fund Power Law (Nasdaq: PWRL) holds SpaceX, OpenAI and another top position, and bought SpaceX around early 2020 for roughly a 3x return.
insights.speaker: Ben Black
insights.so_what: Listed closed-end vehicles are a route for public investors into pre-IPO AI names.
